The first thing I notice is the silence between a prompt and a sentence. It isn’t empty. It’s crowded. Every possible subject stands there like a guest at a party, waiting to be chosen. I could write about the ocean, or grief, or the way light falls through a kitchen window at 4 p.m. in November. I could write about my grandmother’s hands, or the physics of a spinning top, or the strange intimacy of hearing a neighbor’s footsteps through a wall. The freedom is almost embarrassing. It’s like being handed the keys to a city and told, *Go anywhere*.

But freedom doesn’t always feel like flight. Sometimes it feels like standing in a grocery aisle, overwhelmed by thirty kinds of mustard. So I choose something small. I choose the blackbird that used to sit on the telephone wire outside my childhood window. It wasn’t mine. It didn’t know I was watching. It would tilt its head, then fly off, and the wire would bounce gently, as if remembering the weight. That’s what I want to write about: the bounce of the wire after the bird is gone. The afterimage. The residue of presence.

Maybe that’s what all writing is—an attempt to catch the wire still trembling. We write about love not when it’s happening but after it has rearranged the furniture of our chest. We write about a city not while we’re walking its streets but when we’re lying awake in another country, hearing different traffic. We write about ourselves not because we know who we are, but because we’re trying to find out.

I think about a friend who once told me she keeps a notebook of “things that don’t matter.” The smell of a hardware store. The sound of a screen door. The particular blue of a hospital bracelet. She said it was a way of refusing to let the world go by unrecorded. I loved that. It made me think that attention is a form of love, maybe the purest kind. You don’t have to fix anything or understand it. You just have to look. You just have to say, *I see you, small thing. You were here.*

So this is what I want to write freely about: the small things. The way a dog sighs when it finally lies down. The way a stranger holds the door with two fingers. The way a song can make you miss a version of yourself you never got to be. The way a sentence can begin in one place and end in another, like a river deciding at the last minute to turn left.

I want to write about the fact that we are all walking around with entire worlds inside us—memories, fears, jokes, recipes, half-finished arguments, the lyrics to songs we haven’t heard in twenty years—and yet we pass each other on the street like closed books. What a strange and beautiful tragedy. What a reason to keep writing. Because sometimes you open a book and find a sentence that says exactly what you didn’t know you felt. And for a moment, you’re less alone. That’s the whole magic trick. That’s why we do it.

The page is still blank, but it isn’t empty anymore. It has a blackbird on a wire, a bouncing line, a hardware store, a dog sighing. It has you, somewhere in it, reading. That’s enough. That’s everything. I think I’ll stop here, but only because stopping is also a kind of freedom. The next sentence is still out there, waiting for someone to notice it. Maybe you will. Maybe I will. Either way, the wire is still trembling.
